rationale:
Evidence: iteration 7 is the best design so far (344.5). The plant change worked. Its oval result was 17 of 20 finishes, mean progress 0.95, and mean finish time 1.86 s. Its s-bend and slalom results were still failures: progress 0.34 and 0.11, with 1.15 and 1.25 line-loss events per run. Steering oscillation rose to 0.22 on the s-bend, and control effort was 5.4. The likely pattern is that the lower yaw inertia and narrower track now let the robot turn fast enough to overshoot on tight alternating bends, so it oscillates and drifts off the tape.

Changes, chosen to continue the plant-response direction and add damping. (1) Reduce wheel_track from 0.10 to 0.09 m, giving about 11 percent more yaw rate per unit wheel differential so the robot can follow the tighter slalom bends. (2) Reduce mass from 0.6 to 0.5 kg. This lowers yaw inertia further, which helps the robot change direction quickly. (3) Raise kd from 0.6 to 0.8 to damp the overshoot that produced the higher oscillation on the s-bend and slalom. (4) Keep kp at 2.0 and ki at 0.1, since the kp change in iteration 6 showed no effect and the motor-mismatch correction is still useful. (5) Keep base_speed at 1.3 so finishing time stays near 1.9 s, and keep the sensor array (8 mm footprint, x = -0.016 to +0.016 m, y = 0.06 m), body and wheel radius unchanged, so the effect of the plant change is isolated from sensing.

Expected result: lower steering_oscillation (target below 0.15) and fewer line-loss events on the s-bend and slalom, with s-bend progress rising above 0.5. Oval completions should stay at or above the current rate. The main risk is that the faster yaw response overshoots more, which the extra kd is intended to counter. The next telemetry should show whether oscillation fell and whether the slalom now gets past its first bends.
